pharm: Competitively blocks peripheral muscarinic receptors, reducing secretions, gastric acid, and vagal tone; as a quaternary amine it poorly crosses the blood-brain barrier.
quick: Preanesthetic 0.004 mg/kg IM; intraoperative 0.1 mg IV repeated q2-3 min as needed
Oral forms: take on an empty stomach; injection unrelated to meals
Limited data; use only if clearly needed
May suppress lactation; quaternary structure limits milk transfer
Use with caution; renally eliminated, may accumulate
No specific interaction; avoid additive CNS effects with other drugs
Heart rate, anticholinergic effects, intraocular pressure in at-risk patients
summary: Glycopyrrolate is a synthetic quaternary anticholinergic used in anesthesia to reduce salivary, tracheobronchial and pharyngeal secretions, to block cardiac vagal reflexes, to reverse the muscarinic effects of cholinergic agents (with neostigmine/pyridostigmine), and as an adjunct in peptic ulcer when a rapid antisecretory effect is desired. Because it is a quaternary amine, central anticholinergic effects are minimal.
indications: Preanesthetic reduction of salivary, tracheobronchial and pharyngeal secretions and gastric secretion volume/acidity, and blockade of cardiac inhibitory reflexes
Protection against peripheral muscarinic effects during reversal of neuromuscular blockade
Adjunct to reduce symptoms of peptic ulcer when rapid anticholinergic effect is needed (not monotherapy)

dosage.d: 0.004 mg/kg IM 30-60 min before induction (children <2 yr may need up to 0.009 mg/kg)
0.1 mg IV, repeat at 2-3 min intervals as needed
0.2 mg IV for each 1 mg neostigmine or 5 mg pyridostigmine
dosage.n: Give together or just before the anticholinesterase

dosage.d: 0.1 mg IV or IM at 4-hour intervals, 3-4 times daily
dosage.n: Not indicated as monotherapy; not for pediatric peptic ulcer

admin: May be given IM or IV without dilution
Inspect for particulate matter and discoloration before use
When used to reverse neuromuscular blockade, administer with the anticholinesterase to blunt muscarinic effects
Monitor heart rate during IV use
moa: Glycopyrrolate competitively inhibits acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors of smooth muscle, secretory glands, and the SA/AV nodes. This reduces salivary, bronchial and gastric secretions, lowers gastric acidity, and blocks vagal slowing of the heart, producing antisecretory and modest positive-chronotropic effects. Its quaternary ammonium structure limits passage across the blood-brain barrier and the placenta.

absolute: For oral/peptic-ulcer use: glaucoma, obstructive uropathy (e.g., bladder neck obstruction from prostatic hypertrophy), obstructive GI disease (achalasia, pyloroduodenal stenosis)
Paralytic ileus, intestinal atony in elderly/debilitated patients
Unstable cardiovascular status in acute hemorrhage
relative: Coronary artery disease, tachyarrhythmias, hyperthyroidism, hypertension
monitor: Signs of urinary retention or constipation

preg: Animal data are limited and there are no adequate well-controlled human studies; as a quaternary amine placental transfer is low. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk.
lact: It is not known whether glycopyrrolate is excreted in human milk; anticholinergics may suppress lactation. Use with caution and observe the infant for anticholinergic effects.
renal: Glycopyrrolate is substantially eliminated by the kidney; impaired renal function may decrease clearance and prolong effect. Use with caution and consider lower or less frequent dosing.
hepatic: No specific dosage adjustment is established; use with caution in significant hepatic impairment.

major: Potassium chloride solid oral dosage forms (anticholinergic delay of GI transit increases risk of upper-GI ulceration)
moderate: Other anticholinergics/antimuscarinics (additive effects: dry mouth, urinary retention, ileus)
Antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, phenothiazines (additive anticholinergic load)
minor: Antacids (may reduce absorption of oral glycopyrrolate; separate dosing)
interactions.food: Oral forms should be taken on an empty stomach; food can reduce absorption.
interactions.alcohol: No direct interaction, but additive sedation possible with other CNS depressants.
interactions.diagnostics: May increase intraocular pressure; interferes with gastric acid studies.

serious: Heat prostration (in high temperatures due to decreased sweating)
rare: Psychosis or confusion (mainly elderly, high doses)

monitoring: Heart rate and rhythm during IV administration
Intraocular pressure in patients at risk of glaucoma
Bowel and bladder function with repeated dosing
counsel: Expect dry mouth and reduced sweating; avoid overheating and strenuous activity in hot weather
Report difficulty urinating, severe constipation, eye pain, or palpitations
For oral forms, take on an empty stomach
pk: Antisialagogue effect up to ~7 hours; vagal-blocking 2-3 hours
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from light; do not freeze
pearls: Quaternary structure means minimal CNS penetration, so unlike atropine it rarely causes central anticholinergic delirium
Preferred over atropine in some settings because of fewer CNS effects and longer antisialagogue action
Paired with neostigmine/pyridostigmine to prevent bradycardia during neuromuscular-blockade reversal
Reduces gastric acidity and volume, useful before anesthesia to lower aspiration risk
missed: For scheduled antisecretory dosing, give the missed dose when remembered unless it is nearly time for the next; do not double. Procedural/intraoperative doses are given by clinicians as needed.
overdose: Overdose produces an intensified peripheral anticholinergic syndrome: marked tachycardia, urinary retention, hyperthermia, flushing, dry skin, and circulatory failure; central effects are uncommon due to limited CNS penetration. Management is supportive with cooling, fluids, and bladder catheterization; physostigmine may reverse severe peripheral effects, and the curare-like action at high doses may require respiratory support.
